title: India Turns to Diaspora in Nagoya as Asian Games Accommodation Crisis Deepens
excerpt: With athletes evacuated from flooded container rooms and India's shooting team left waiting until 3 a.m., some 2,000 Indians in Nagoya stand ready to open their homes.
body:
• India's Sports Ministry has activated a three-tier management system for the Nagoya Asian Games, with roughly 2,000 members of the Indian community in Japan ready to host athletes facing accommodation problems.
  • The move follows widespread chaos: athletes evacuated from flooded container-style rooms, and India's 35-member shooting contingent arriving at 3 a.m. to find only seven rooms booked.
  • Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya met IOA president PT Usha in Nagoya, while chef de mission Sahdev Yadav admitted "there is definitely a shortage of accommodation."
  • The Asian Games open September 19 with more than 17,000 athletes and officials — the largest field ever — housed in hotels, a cruise ship and temporary container units instead of a village.

As the Asian Games open in Nagoya, India's sports establishment is turning to an unusual line of defence against the organising committee's logistical collapse: the diaspora. The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports has put a three-tier management framework in place, and about 2,000 members of the Indian community in Japan are prepared to open their homes to athletes if necessary.

A ministry source said the community members are on standby for accommodation, transport and other essential services. Two diaspora representatives are stationed at the airport and three at the welcome centre, working alongside chef de mission Sahdev Yadav and Sports Authority of India officials.

A shortage nobody planned for

India's chef de mission acknowledged the crisis publicly. Sahdev Yadav told reporters the contingent had to book additional hotel rooms after its accommodation quota was cut on arrival. "Everyone has accommodation, and there is no problem from our side. There were some issues initially, which is why we booked an additional hotel... There is definitely a shortage of accommodation," he said.

The admission followed a brutal opening week for India's teams. The 35-member shooting contingent landed in Nagoya at 9 p.m. on September 15, waited at an accreditation centre from 11:45 p.m. until 3 a.m. without transport, and then discovered only seven rooms had been reserved for 35 people. The IOA intervened to secure 18 rooms across two properties, and athletes carried luggage and shooting equipment between them on foot until 5:30 a.m. A training bus the next morning arrived more than three hours late.

Elsewhere, record rainfall forced hundreds of athletes to be evacuated from the Garden Pier container accommodation after flooding. Indian shot put champion Tajinderpal Singh Toor was seen settling into one of the container units himself.

No village, no fallback

The 20th Asian Games, running September 19 to October 4, dispensed with a traditional athletes' village to cut costs. More than 17,000 registered athletes and officials — a number bigger than the Olympics — are instead spread across hotels, a docked cruise ship and temporary wooden container-style units expected to house about 2,000 participants.

The Olympic Council of Asia said Friday that all athletes and officials registered by the entry deadline had been given Games-appropriate accommodation, while conceding logistical strains. Organisers admitted they had anticipated "challenges" and prepared backup hotels.

India tried to prepare for exactly this scenario. The SAI built replica 40-foot container units at training centres in Patiala and Bengaluru and ran athletes through overnight stays to remove the shock of cramped quarters. That preparation did not cover flooded rooms and missing buses.

Political cover from the top

Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya travelled to Nagoya and met IOA president PT Usha, who posted that his presence "will undoubtedly uplift our contingent's morale." For the diaspora, the mobilisation is a point of pride — an immigrant community stepping in where the host organisation faltered, days before their adopted home city goes under the global spotlight.

The athletics programme runs September 23 to 29. Whether medals follow will depend on preparation surviving the journey — and on whether 2,000 open doors in Nagoya stay unneeded.
image_caption: Nagoya at night, host city of the 2026 Asian Games. The city is facing an accommodation crunch that has pushed India to lean on its diaspora.
nri_angle: The Indian diaspora in Japan is literally opening its homes to athletes, turning a host-organiser failure into a showcase of community mobilization.
